patients.summary: Retired postal clerk with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, CKD 3a, BPH and chronic lumbar stenosis on pain-clinic morphine who joins in 2015. Over the next decade he has a TIA, cervical myelopathy, Waldenström macroglobulinemia, then AL amyloidosis, normal pressure hydrocephalus, vascular dementia and two lacunar strokes, with outside letters that often arrive late.

documents.title: New Patient Visit and Initial Preventive Exam
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
65 y/o retired postal clerk here to establish care. Prior PCP retired; records requested.

HPI: Diabetes for roughly seven years, on metformin 1000 twice a day; says his last A1c 'was around 7.' BP treated for about ten years with lisinopril and HCTZ; doesn't check at home. Prostate: gets up twice a night, stream okay on tamsulosin. Back: lumbar stenosis, aching low back and buttocks with standing and walking, better sitting; followed by an outside pain clinic for several years, which prescribes long-acting morphine 60 twice daily and short-acting 15 for bad days (uses 1-2 a day). Neck stiffness for years, told it was arthritis in the neck. Told by old PCP his kidney numbers were 'a little low.'

PMH: HTN, T2DM, CKD 3a, BPH, lumbar spinal stenosis, cervical spondylosis, hyperlipidemia.
PSH: none.
Meds: metformin 1000 BID, lisinopril 20 daily, HCTZ 12.5 daily, tamsulosin 0.4 qhs, atorvastatin 40 qhs; morphine ER 60 q12h and morphine IR 15 q4h prn (pain clinic).
Allergies: sulfa antibiotics (hives); IV contrast dye (anaphylaxis, needed epinephrine during a CT years ago).
FH: father had an ischemic stroke at 74. Mother had diabetes and high blood pressure. Maternal uncle had Waldenström macroglobulinemia, found in his early 70s. Sister has osteoarthritis.
SH: lives with his wife in Deerfield. Retired from the postal service. Quit cigarettes in 2010, about 25 pack-years. 1-2 beers on weekends. No other substances.

ROS: no chest pain, no shortness of breath, no weakness or numbness, no blood in urine, no falls.

Exam: BP and vitals as recorded. Alert, pleasant. Fundi not well seen through undilated pupils. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, no bruit. Lumbar paraspinal tenderness, forward flexion limited by pain. Neck rotation mildly reduced both ways. Strength full in arms and legs, reflexes 2+ and symmetric, toes down. Feet: monofilament intact, pulses 2+, no ulcers or calluses. Gait normal.

Welcome exam: vision screen done, hearing okay to whisper, PHQ-2 0, no falls in past year, home safe, wife at home. Advance directive: not yet; handout given.

A/P:
1. T2DM with CKD 3a: A1c, CMP, urine albumin/creatinine today. Continue metformin.
2. HTN: at goal today. Continue lisinopril/HCTZ.
3. Hyperlipidemia: lipids today, continue atorvastatin 40.
4. Lumbar stenosis on chronic opioids: pain clinic manages. Will keep their letters on file.
5. BPH: PSA after discussion, he wants it.
6. Prevention: Tdap and PCV13 today. Hep C screen once. Old colonoscopy report to come with records. Flu shot next month when stocked.
Return 3 months.

documents.title: Your lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Mr. Mayhew, welcome again. Your A1c is 7.1, close to where we want it. Kidney function (creatinine 1.36) puts you at the same stage 3a your prior doctor described, and there is a small amount of protein in the urine (42), which the lisinopril helps with. Cholesterol, blood count and PSA were fine, and the hepatitis C screen was negative. No changes. See you in December.

documents.body:
OUTSIDE PAIN MANAGEMENT CLINIC — Annual summary to new PCP
Re: Dennis Mayhew, DOB 07/19/1950

Thank you for taking over his primary care. He has been with our clinic for lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication, managed on a stable opioid regimen: morphine sulfate ER 60 mg every 12 hours plus morphine IR 15 mg up to every 4 hours as needed. Controlled substance agreement on file; urine drug testing consistent; state monitoring program reviewed each fill. Function: walks about 15 minutes at a time, does light yard work.

Allergies: sulfonamide antibiotics (hives), iodinated contrast (anaphylaxis).

We see him every 3 months and write all opioid prescriptions. Please do not prescribe opioids. We would appreciate yearly kidney function results.

Pain management physician

documents.title: Post-ED visit: TIA
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Here with wife. On 11/7 at home, about 20 min of word-finding difficulty and right-hand clumsiness, fully resolved before ED arrival. Per their discharge sheet: head CT without contrast normal, carotid ultrasound without significant narrowing, ECG sinus rhythm. No MRI (they did not offer one). Started aspirin 81 there. No recurrence. No headache, no vision loss.
Exam: alert, fluent speech, naming and repetition intact. Cranial nerves normal. Strength 5/5 throughout, fine finger movements equal, reflexes symmetric, toes down. Heart regular, no murmur, no carotid bruits.
A/P: TIA, now resolved. Continue aspirin 81 daily. Already on atorvastatin 40; continue. BP fine today. Diabetes as before. Full ED record requested. Stroke warning signs reviewed with both of them.

reports.text:
Indication: transient aphasia and right hand weakness.
Technique: Noncontrast axial CT of the head.
Findings: No acute hemorrhage, mass or territorial infarct. Gray-white differentiation preserved. Ventricles and sulci appropriate for age. No extra-axial collection. Calvarium intact.

Bilateral common, internal and external carotid arteries evaluated. Mild smooth plaque at both carotid bulbs. Velocities in the internal carotid arteries within normal limits bilaterally. Antegrade vertebral flow bilaterally.
reports.conclusion: No hemodynamically significant carotid stenosis (less than 50% bilaterally).

documents.author: urology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE UROLOGY GROUP — Consultation and procedure note, 04/20/2018
Reason: persistent microscopic hematuria. 67M, former smoker (25 pk-yr, quit 2010), BPH on tamsulosin. Renal ultrasound from PCP reviewed: normal kidneys, enlarged prostate. CT urography avoided because of contrast anaphylaxis.
Allergies: sulfonamide antibiotics (hives), iodinated contrast (anaphylaxis).
Procedure: Flexible diagnostic cystoscopy under local anesthetic. Urethra normal. Prostate with enlarged, coapting lateral lobes. Bladder mucosa normal throughout with no tumor, stone, or diverticulum. Ureteral orifices normal in position with clear efflux.
Impression: Microscopic hematuria, no bladder pathology. Likely related to prostatic enlargement.
Plan: Continue tamsulosin. Repeat UA with routine care; return for any visible blood.
Urologist

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: About 3 months of worsening neck pain. When he bends his head down he gets an electric jolt down his back. Walking feels harder, 'like my legs don't listen.' Different from his usual lumbar pain. No falls, no bladder change, no trauma.
O: Vitals as charted. Neck flexion reproduces the shock sensation. Grip seems weaker than I recall; knee reflexes brisk. Gait slightly wide. Exam otherwise as before.
A/P: Neck pain with shock sensations on flexion and gait change in a man with known cervical spondylosis: concern for cervical cord compression. Neurology referral, urgent slot requested; they will order MRI (no contrast needed; gadolinium not the same as his iodine allergy, but they can decide). Return precautions for weakness, falls or bladder change.

documents.title: Neurology consultation, 06/04/2019
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE NEUROLOGY — Consultation letter, visit 06/04/2019

Dear colleague,
Thank you for referring Mr. Mayhew, 68, with half a year of increasing neck pain, a harder time walking, and shock-like sensations running down his back whenever he flexes his neck. This began roughly six months after his last pain-clinic review of his lumbar stenosis. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes.
Medications: metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg, HCTZ 12.5 mg, tamsulosin 0.4 mg qhs, morphine ER 60 mg BID, morphine IR 15 mg q4h prn, atorvastatin 40 mg, aspirin 81 mg.
Allergies: sulfonamide antibiotics (hives), iodinated contrast (anaphylaxis).

Examination: Wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles bilaterally with reduced grip. Biceps and triceps jerks reduced. Knee jerks 3+, with sustained clonus at both ankles. Right plantar response extensor; left flexor.

Recent labs from your office: A1c 7.2%, fasting glucose 156, total cholesterol 210, HDL 40, LDL 130, triglycerides 200.

MRI cervical spine without contrast (06/04/2019): multilevel degenerative disease with disc-osteophyte complexes narrowing the spinal canal at several levels.

Impression: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy, multilevel.
Plan: Referral to spine surgery to discuss decompression. Fall precautions. Neurology follow-up after the surgical opinion.

Neurologist

documents.title: Spine surgery consultation, 07/22/2019
documents.author: spine surgery
documents.body:
OUTSIDE SPINE SURGERY — Consultation, 07/22/2019
Referred by neurology for cervical spondylotic myelopathy. 69M with neck pain, gait difficulty and flexion-induced shocks; MRI with multilevel degenerative canal narrowing. Exam today consistent with the neurology findings: hand intrinsic wasting, hyperreflexia in the legs with ankle clonus.
Allergies: sulfonamide antibiotics, iodinated contrast.
Discussion: We reviewed multilevel posterior decompression versus nonoperative management with close surveillance, including risks of surgery at his age with diabetes and chronic opioid use, and the risk of progression without surgery. After discussion with his wife he prefers nonoperative care for now.
Plan: Nonoperative management. Physical therapy for balance and gait. Avoid neck manipulation. Neurology to follow; return to us for any decline in hand function, walking or bladder control.
Spine surgeon

documents.author: PCP

S: Two months of blurry vision in both eyes (not just the cataract eye), dull headaches most days, spells of dizziness lasting minutes, and pins and needles in the hands and feet. Not the same as his neck shocks. No new weakness, no speech trouble, no falls. No fevers, no night sweats.

orders.reason: monoclonal protein 3.4 g/dL, anemia, possible hyperviscosity symptoms

documents.title: Results call: monoclonal protein
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Called pt and wife. SPEP shows a monoclonal spike, 3.4 g/dL in the gamma region; immunofixation typing to follow. Together with the anemia, high protein and his vision and headache symptoms, I am worried about a blood protein disorder that can thicken the blood. Spoke directly with hematology-oncology on call; they will see him 6/5, sooner if symptoms worsen. Told them to go to the ED for confusion, worsening vision, bleeding, or severe headache. Wife mentioned his uncle had 'a blood protein cancer.' They understand.

reports.text:
Specimen: Bone marrow aspirate and core biopsy, right posterior iliac crest.
Microscopic: Hypercellular marrow with an interstitial and nodular infiltrate of small lymphocytes, many with plasmacytoid features, admixed with plasma cells. Trilineage hematopoiesis present but reduced. Flow cytometry: monotypic B-cell population with lambda light chain restriction. Molecular: MYD88 L265P mutation detected.
reports.conclusion: Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma involving bone marrow, consistent with Waldenström macroglobulinemia in the setting of an IgM lambda paraprotein.

documents.title: Hematology-oncology consultation, 06/05/2020

OUTSIDE CANCER CENTER, HEMATOLOGY-ONCOLOGY — New patient consultation, 06/05/2020

Referred for monoclonal protein and anemia. 69M with cervical myelopathy and lumbar stenosis (followed by neurology and pain management), HTN and T2DM on metformin and lisinopril. Two months of blurred vision, headaches, dizzy spells, and tingling in hands and feet.
Allergies: sulfonamide antibiotics (hives), iodinated contrast (anaphylaxis).
Family history: maternal uncle with Waldenström macroglobulinemia.

Exam: Pale conjunctivae. Fundoscopy shows engorged retinal veins bilaterally. Diminished light-touch sensation in a stocking-glove distribution.

Data: PCP labs 05/19: Hgb 10.2, MCV 89, creatinine 1.4, calcium 9.2, total protein 9.8, albumin 3.2, M-spike 3.4 g/dL (gamma). Today: IgM 4,850 mg/dL; immunofixation IgM lambda; serum viscosity elevated at 4.8 cP. Bone marrow biopsy performed today (report attached).

Assessment: Waldenström macroglobulinemia with symptomatic hyperviscosity and anemia.
Plan: Plasma exchange as soon as arranged, then bendamustine plus rituximab every 28 days for six cycles. Hold off on any rituximab until IgM is lowered. Will keep you updated.
Hematology-oncology physician

reports.text:
Indication: AL amyloidosis evaluation, orthopnea, edema.
Left ventricle: normal cavity size. Increased wall thickness, concentric. Systolic function preserved, LVEF estimated 55%. Diastolic assessment: mitral inflow and tissue velocity measurements indicate a restrictive filling pattern.
Right ventricle: normal size, wall thickened, function preserved.
Atria: normal size.
Valves: structurally normal aortic and mitral valves.
Pericardium: no effusion.
reports.conclusion: Increased ventricular wall thickness with normal chamber size and restrictive filling, consistent with infiltrative cardiomyopathy in the setting of AL amyloidosis.

reports.text: Liver enlarged, measuring 19.5 cm craniocaudal at the midclavicular line, homogeneous echotexture, no focal lesion. No intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary dilatation. Gallbladder normal. Pancreas partly obscured. Spleen normal size. Kidneys normal size without hydronephrosis. No ascites.

documents.author: hematology-oncology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE CANCER CENTER, HEMATOLOGY-ONCOLOGY — Follow-up and new diagnosis, 06/04/2021
(Received by fax 07/19/2021 after two requests.)

Interval: Waldenström macroglobulinemia on observation after bendamustine-rituximab. Three months of progressive fatigue, swelling of both legs, weight loss without trying, orthopnea, and frothy urine. PCP's 5/24 labs reviewed.
Medications: lisinopril 20 mg, tamsulosin 0.4 mg, morphine ER 60 mg BID, morphine IR 15 mg prn, atorvastatin 40 mg, aspirin 81 mg, HCTZ, metformin.
Allergies: sulfonamide antibiotics (hives), iodinated contrast (anaphylaxis).

Vitals: BP 150/90, HR 88, RR 18.
Exam: Low-pitched rumbling diastolic murmur. Striking purpura around both eyes. Pitting edema to the knees bilaterally.

Labs: albumin 2.8, creatinine 1.9, 24-hour urine protein 4.5 g, total cholesterol 260. Liver tests mildly elevated: alkaline phosphatase 196, AST 44, ALT 39. Free lambda light chain 212 mg/L, free kappa 15.4 mg/L. NT-proBNP 2,870 pg/mL.
Abdominal fat pad aspirate: amyloid deposits present; typed as AL lambda.
Echo and abdominal ultrasound: reports attached.

Assessment: AL (lambda) amyloidosis with kidney (nephrotic-range proteinuria), heart and liver involvement, arising from his lymphoplasmacytic clone.
Plan:
- Bortezomib (subcutaneous weekly), dexamethasone and rituximab, 28-day cycles x6, starting this month.
- Acyclovir 400 mg twice daily for zoster prophylaxis during bortezomib.
- Furosemide 40 mg daily for edema; daily weights, low-sodium diet.
- Dexamethasone will raise his sugars; please follow glucose.
Hematology-oncology physician

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Here with daughter Kristen. Since about spring: forgetting conversations and appointments, repeating questions, walking more unsteady (shuffling, 'feet stuck'), and leaking urine before reaching the bathroom. He used to manage his own pills and bills; now wife and daughter help with dressing, bathing and medicines. He minimizes, says he's 'just slower.' No falls with injury. No fever, no new medicines.
Exam: vitals as charted. Alert, pleasant, recall 1/3 at 5 minutes, clock drawing disorganized. Gait slow, wide-based, short steps; turns in several steps. Strength in legs full. Reflexes as before.
A/P: Triad of cognitive decline, gait change and urinary incontinence over ~6 months. Differential includes normal pressure hydrocephalus, vascular disease (prior TIA), progression of cervical myelopathy, medication effect (opioids). B12, TSH, BMP and UA today. Neurology referral, prior neurologist's office. Fall safety, supervised meds. Daughter to keep a list of episodes.

reports.text:
Indication: memory loss, gait instability, incontinence.
Technique: Noncontrast axial CT of the head.
Findings: Lateral and third ventricles are enlarged out of proportion to the cortical sulci, which are normal in size. No acute hemorrhage, mass, or territorial infarct. No extra-axial collection. Postoperative change of the left lens.
reports.conclusion: Ventriculomegaly with normal-sized sulci. Clinical correlation for normal pressure hydrocephalus.

documents.title: Neurology consultation, 11/21/2022
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE NEUROLOGY — Consultation, 11/21/2022
Seen with his daughter for six months of worsening memory, unsteady walking and urinary incontinence; previously independent, he now needs help with daily activities. Known to us for cervical spondylotic myelopathy (nonoperative). Also Waldenström macroglobulinemia and AL amyloidosis.
Medications: metformin, lisinopril, HCTZ, tamsulosin, morphine ER and IR, atorvastatin, aspirin, furosemide.
Allergies: sulfonamide antibiotics, iodinated contrast.
Exam: Wide-based gait with feet that seem stuck to the floor; cannot do tandem walking. No weakness. Sensation intact. MMSE 24/30.
CT head without contrast today: large ventricles with normal sulci (report attached).
Impression: Normal pressure hydrocephalus with mild cognitive impairment.
Plan: High-volume lumbar tap test with timed walking before and after; decide on shunt referral based on the response.
Neurologist

documents.title: Lumbar tap test, 01/17/2023
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE NEUROLOGY — Procedure and follow-up note
Procedure (01/17/2023): High-volume lumbar puncture, L3-4, lateral decubitus, sterile technique, no complications. Aspirin not held. Opening pressure 13 cm H2O. 35 mL clear CSF removed.
Assessment: 10-meter walk 21 seconds before, 18 seconds at 3 hours after. MMSE unchanged. Daughter felt he walked 'a little lighter' that afternoon only.
Impression: Modest response. Given AL amyloidosis with cardiac involvement, frailty and the small improvement, we and the family agreed not to pursue shunt surgery.
Plan: Physical therapy for gait and balance; walker for distances; follow up in neurology clinic in a year or sooner for change.
Neurologist

Indication: acute involuntary movements of left arm and leg.
Technique: Noncontrast axial CT of the head.
Findings: Small area of hyperdensity in the deep structures of the right cerebral hemisphere. Multiple small chronic hypodensities in the subcortical white matter and both basal ganglia, unchanged. Enlarged ventricles, unchanged. No hemorrhage elsewhere, no mass effect, no extra-axial collection.
reports.conclusion: Small right deep hemispheric hyperdensity, consistent with acute lacunar infarct. Chronic small vessel changes and ventriculomegaly unchanged.

documents.title: Emergency department record, 03/29/2025
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT — Physician record, 03/29/2025 (received 04/03/2025)
CC: involuntary flinging movements, left side.
HPI: 74M with cervical spondylotic myelopathy, Waldenström macroglobulinemia and vascular dementia, brought by his wife after large, unpredictable flinging movements of the left arm and leg began earlier today and worsened through the afternoon; unable to walk or feed himself. Never had anything like this before. Hypertension and diabetes, both poorly controlled; reports not taking lisinopril or metformin for several months.
Home meds per list: HCTZ 12.5 mg, tamsulosin 0.4 mg, morphine ER 60 mg BID, morphine IR 15 mg prn, atorvastatin 40 mg, aspirin 81 mg; lisinopril and metformin prescribed but not taken.
Allergies: sulfonamide antibiotics (hives); iodinated contrast (anaphylaxis) — no CT angiography.
Exam: Alert and oriented. Continuous, irregular, large-amplitude movements of the left arm and leg. Tone hard to judge with the movements; no spasticity or rigidity. Reflexes symmetric. No pronator drift. Sensation intact. Cranial nerves intact.
Fingerstick glucose 214.
Noncontrast head CT: report attached.
Impression: Left hemiballism (chorea) from acute right lacunar infarct.
Disposition: Admitted to the hospital medicine service with neurology consultation.
ED physician

Indication: acute right-sided weakness.
Technique: Multiplanar multisequence MRI of the brain without contrast, including diffusion-weighted imaging.
Findings: Small focus of restricted diffusion in a deep location, consistent with an acute lacunar infarct. Chronic small vessel changes in the subcortical white matter and basal ganglia. Ventriculomegaly, unchanged. No hemorrhage, mass or extra-axial collection.

CC: sudden right-sided weakness.
History: 75M with WM, AL amyloidosis, NPH, vascular dementia, prior right lacunar infarct with left hemiballism (2025), HTN, T2DM, CKD 3a.
Home meds: metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg, HCTZ 12.5 mg, tamsulosin 0.4 mg, morphine ER 60 mg BID, morphine IR 15 mg prn, atorvastatin 40 mg, aspirin 81 mg.
Allergies: sulfonamide antibiotics (hives); iodinated contrast (anaphylaxis).
Exam: Weakness of the right face, arm and leg, equally reduced in proximal and distal muscles. Sensation, coordination, language and cranial nerves otherwise normal.
MRI brain: small lacunar infarct (report attached).
Impression: Acute lacunar infarct with pure motor right hemiparesis.
Disposition: ED observation overnight; therapy evaluation; discharged home 03/21 with home PT and PCP follow-up.
